metadata.description:
For more than two thousand years, armies, fleets and empires fought to control one city: Byzantium, then Constantinople, now Istanbul. Why this one?

In this video: the Bosphorus, the narrow strait between Europe and Asia that controls the only sea route out of the Black Sea, the Greek colonists who chose the site, Constantine's New Rome, walls that held for a thousand years, the fall of the city in 1453, why Russia and Britain fought over the straits, and why the strait still matters today.
metadata.pinned_comment: Constantinople or Istanbul: which name do you use when you talk about the city's history? 👇

scenes.narration: This is Istanbul. The only great city in the world that sits on two continents at once.
For more than two thousand years, it has been a prize that empires were willing to fight for, again and again.

data.text: A prize empires fought for, again and again

scenes.narration: Persians, Avars, Arabs, Bulgarians, Rus warriors, crusaders and Ottomans all came to its walls.
And the reason is right here: a narrow strip of water, just a few hundred meters wide at one point.
So why did every empire want this one city?

data.text: Why did every empire want this city?

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you'll see how one strait, one harbor and one set of walls made this the most valuable piece of land between Europe and Asia.

data.text: One strait, one harbor, one set of walls

scenes.narration: Today, Istanbul is home to around fifteen and a half million people. It's by far the largest city in Turkey, and one of the largest in Europe.
To understand why it matters so much, zoom out. North of Istanbul is the Black Sea, a sea almost as big as Spain, surrounded by land.
The Black Sea has only one way out to the oceans. And that way runs straight through the middle of Istanbul.

data.text: One way out of the Black Sea

scenes.narration: Ships leaving the Black Sea must pass through the Bosphorus, then cross the small Sea of Marmara, then pass a second strait, the Dardanelles, before reaching the Aegean and the Mediterranean.
The Bosphorus is about thirty kilometers long. At its narrowest, it's only around seven hundred meters wide. You could almost shout across it.
Whoever holds this city holds the gate. They can let ships pass, charge them for passing, or stop them completely.
And the Bosphorus isn't only a sea route. It's also the shortest crossing between Europe and Asia. Armies and traders traveling by land have crossed here since ancient times.

data.text: A sea route and a land bridge at the same time

scenes.narration: So the city sits on a crossroads. Ships go north and south, between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. People and goods go east and west, between Europe and Asia.
Then there's the Golden Horn, a long, sheltered inlet on the European side. It's one of the best natural harbors in the whole Mediterranean world.

data.text: One of the best natural harbors in the world

scenes.narration: Add a peninsula with water on three sides, and you get a city that is easy to supply by sea and hard to attack by land. Perfect for trade, and perfect for defense.

data.text: Easy to supply, hard to attack

scenes.narration: Even the currents help the city. Huge rivers like the Danube pour fresh water into the Black Sea, so a strong surface current flows out through the Bosphorus. Ships sailing north have to fight against it.
So who first noticed what a perfect place this was? The answer involves a famous insult.

data.text: It begins with a famous insult

scenes.narration: In the seventh century BC, Greek colonists from the city of Megara sailed here. First they founded Chalcedon, on the Asian shore. Some years later, others founded Byzantium, on the European side.
Look at the two sites. Chalcedon had no great harbor. Byzantium had the Golden Horn, and a peninsula that was much easier to defend.
According to the Greek historian Herodotus, a Persian general later said the people of Chalcedon must have been blind, to settle there when the better site was right in front of them.

data.text: The people of Chalcedon must have been blind.
data.author: A Persian general, as told by Herodotus

scenes.narration: Byzantium grew rich from the strait. In ancient times, huge amounts of grain from the lands around the Black Sea passed through the Bosphorus on their way to the cities of Greece.

data.text: Rich from the grain ships

scenes.narration: Athens, in particular, depended on that grain. Whoever controlled the strait could feed Athens, or starve it.
So for centuries, Byzantium was fought over by Persians, Athenians, Spartans and Macedonians. Even as a small Greek town, it was already a prize.

data.text: Even as a small town, it was a prize

scenes.narration: In 340 BC, Philip of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, besieged Byzantium. Even he failed to take it.
But its real rise came when a Roman emperor decided that this was the place to build the new center of the world.

data.text: A new center of the world

scenes.narration: By the early three hundreds AD, the Roman Empire's main threats were in the east and along the Danube. The city of Rome was simply too far away.
So the emperor Constantine rebuilt Byzantium as his new capital. In the year 330, it was dedicated as New Rome. People soon called it Constantinople, the city of Constantine.

When the western half of the Roman Empire collapsed in the four hundreds, the eastern half survived, ruled from Constantinople. Historians call it the Byzantine Empire, but its people simply called themselves Romans.

data.text: The Roman Empire lived on in the east

scenes.narration: To protect the city, in the early four hundreds, the emperor Theodosius the Second built a new line of walls across the peninsula, from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn.

data.text: A wall from sea to sea

scenes.narration: On the land side, there was only one short front to defend, about six kilometers long. On every other side, the city was protected by water.
And it wasn't one wall. Attackers first faced a wide moat, then an outer wall, then a taller inner wall with nearly a hundred towers.

data.title: Three layers of defense
items: A taller inner wall with towers

scenes.narration: Those walls would protect the city for about a thousand years. Many historians consider them the most successful defensive walls ever built.

data.caption: the strongest walls of the medieval world

scenes.narration: Behind them, Constantinople became the largest and richest city in Europe. In the five hundreds, it may have had around half a million people.

data.text: The richest city in Europe

scenes.narration: Its gold coin, the solidus, was trusted from Western Europe to Persia, and stayed remarkably stable for centuries. Some historians call it the dollar of the Middle Ages.

data.text: The dollar of the Middle Ages

scenes.narration: Crowds of tens of thousands watched chariot races in the Hippodrome. In 532, riots between rival racing fans almost overthrew the emperor Justinian.

data.text: Chariot fans who nearly toppled an emperor

scenes.narration: In 537, the emperor Justinian completed Hagia Sophia. For nearly a thousand years, it was the largest cathedral in the world.
A huge city, an enormous treasury and control of the busiest crossroads in the world. Now every enemy of the empire knew exactly where to aim.

data.text: Every enemy knew where to aim

scenes.narration: In 626, the city was attacked from both sides at once. The Avars came from the European side, while a Persian army waited across the Bosphorus in Asia.
But the two armies needed to join up. And the Byzantine fleet controlled the strait between them. The Persians never crossed, and the siege failed.

data.text: The strait kept the two armies apart

scenes.narration: A few decades later, the armies of the new Arab caliphate arrived. They attacked the city in the 670s, and again in 717, with a huge army and fleet.
The Byzantines had a secret weapon: Greek fire, a liquid that kept burning even on water. It was sprayed onto enemy ships, and its exact recipe is still a mystery today.

data.text: Fire that burned on water

scenes.narration: The great siege of 717 lasted about a year. A harsh winter, disease, and attacks on its fleet forced the Arab army to retreat.
Then, in 860, a fleet of Rus warriors sailed down the rivers of Eastern Europe and across the Black Sea to raid the city's suburbs. The Rus would return several times.
Bulgarian rulers marched to the walls more than once as well. Again and again, the city survived. The walls held, and food kept arriving by sea.

data.text: The walls held. The ships kept coming.

scenes.narration: That was the secret. To take Constantinople, an enemy had to break the land walls and control the sea at the same time. For centuries, no one could do both.

data.title: Why the city was so hard to take

scenes.narration: The first foreign army to break in didn't come from the east at all. It came from Western Europe, and it was supposed to be on the same side.

data.text: The first army to break in came from the west

scenes.narration: In 1204, the Fourth Crusade, which had set out to fight in the Holy Land, turned against Constantinople instead. The crusaders broke in from the Golden Horn and sacked the city.

data.text: SACKED

scenes.narration: Venice, which had supplied the crusaders' ships, took a large share of the treasures. The famous bronze horses that stand in St. Mark's Basilica in Venice were taken from Constantinople.

data.text: The bronze horses of St. Mark's

scenes.narration: Italian merchants moved in for good. Genoa ran its own walled trading colony at Galata, across the Golden Horn. Its Galata Tower, built in 1348, still stands today.

data.text: An Italian colony across the harbor

scenes.narration: The Byzantines retook their city in 1261. But it never recovered its old wealth. And a new power was rising right next door.

data.text: Retaken in 1261, but never the same

scenes.narration: By the 1400s, the Ottoman Turks had conquered almost everything around the city, in Asia and in Europe. Constantinople was an island of Roman rule surrounded by Ottoman land.
Its population had collapsed too. From perhaps half a million people at its height, it now had maybe fifty thousand.
In 1453, the young sultan Mehmed the Second, only twenty-one years old, decided to take it. He had already built a fortress on the Bosphorus to cut off help from the Black Sea.

data.text: A 21-year-old sultan and a fortress on the strait

scenes.narration: His army was many times larger than the defenders, who numbered perhaps seven or eight thousand. And he brought something new: enormous cannons.

data.text: Something the walls had never faced: giant cannons

scenes.narration: One of them was built by a Hungarian engineer called Orban. It could fire stone balls weighing hundreds of kilograms, and it took dozens of oxen to move it.

data.text: Stone balls weighing hundreds of kilograms

scenes.narration: The defenders had blocked the entrance to the Golden Horn with a huge chain stretched across the water. So Mehmed did something astonishing.

data.text: A chain across the harbor

scenes.narration: He had dozens of ships dragged overland, across the hills behind Galata, and launched them into the Golden Horn, behind the chain.

data.text: Warships dragged over the hills

scenes.narration: After about fifty-three days of siege and bombardment, on the twenty-ninth of May, 1453, the Ottoman army broke through the walls. The last Byzantine emperor died in the fighting.
After almost eleven hundred years, the Roman Empire that Constantine had moved here was gone.

data.text: The end of the Roman Empire

scenes.narration: Many historians use 1453 to mark the end of the Middle Ages. Greek scholars who fled to Italy carried ancient texts with them, adding fuel to the Renaissance.

data.text: The end of the Middle Ages

scenes.narration: Mehmed made the city his capital. Hagia Sophia became a mosque, and the city was rebuilt and filled again with people brought in from across the empire.

data.text: A new capital for a new empire

scenes.narration: For the Ottomans, the city was the key to everything. From here, they could rule both their European and Asian lands, and control all trade in and out of the Black Sea.

data.text: The key to two continents

scenes.narration: If you're enjoying this, subscribe. Every week we find the story hidden in another map.

data.text: Subscribe for a new map story every week

chapters.title: The great powers
chapters.title_youtube: The straits and the great powers

scenes.narration: Under the Ottomans, the city grew again. In the 1500s, it was probably the largest city in Europe, filled with mosques, markets and palaces.

data.text: The largest city in Europe, again

scenes.narration: The great architect Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque in the 1550s on one of the city's hills, and the sultans ruled from the Topkapı Palace, overlooking the meeting of the Bosphorus and the Golden Horn.

data.text: Domes and minarets on every hill

scenes.narration: But as the Ottoman Empire weakened, a new power looked at the straits with great interest. Russia.
Russia's southern ports were on the Black Sea. Every Russian warship and grain ship heading for the Mediterranean had to pass through Istanbul, under the guns of another empire.

data.text: Every Russian ship had to pass through Istanbul

scenes.narration: Some Russian thinkers even called the city Tsargrad, the city of the emperor, and dreamed of taking it back for Orthodox Christianity.

data.text: A Russian dream

scenes.narration: Britain and France saw the danger. If Russia controlled the straits, its fleet could sail freely into the Mediterranean, close to their trade routes. So they often backed the Ottomans to keep Russia out.

data.text: Britain and France kept Russia out

scenes.narration: That rivalry was one of the causes of the Crimean War in the 1850s. And in the First World War, the straits were at the center of the fighting again.

In 1915, British and French forces tried to force their way through the Dardanelles and reach Istanbul. The naval attack failed, and the landings at Gallipoli turned into a long, costly campaign before the Allies withdrew.
In secret, the Allies had even agreed that Russia would get the city after the war. But Russia's revolution in 1917 ended that plan.

data.text: The city was secretly promised to Russia

scenes.narration: After the war, Allied troops occupied Istanbul until 1923. When the Republic of Turkey was founded that year, its capital became Ankara, far inland.
Part of the reason was the lesson of history. A capital on the strait was rich, but it was also exposed to every fleet that could reach it.
In 1936, the Montreux Convention set the rules for the straits. Turkey controls them. Merchant ships can pass freely in peacetime, but warships face strict limits.

data.text: STILL IN FORCE

scenes.narration: That treaty is still in force today. And in times of war in the region, it has made Turkey's control of the straits as important as ever.

data.text: A treaty from 1936 that still matters

scenes.narration: Today, tens of thousands of ships pass through the Bosphorus every year, many of them tankers and bulk carriers, sailing right past the city's homes and mosques.

data.text: Tens of thousands of ships every year

scenes.narration: Grain from Ukraine and Russia, and oil from the Black Sea region, still travel this route, just as grain did in the days of ancient Athens.
And the old land bridge is busier than ever. The first bridge across the Bosphorus opened in 1973. Today there are three bridges, a rail tunnel opened in 2013, and a road tunnel opened in 2016.
Every day, huge numbers of people commute between Europe and Asia. For them, changing continents is just the trip to work.

data.text: Changing continents on the way to work

scenes.narration: The city has grown enormously. Around one million people lived here in 1950. Today it's more than fifteen times that.
Even its name tells the story of a crossroads. Istanbul most likely comes from a Greek phrase meaning to the city. It became the city's only official name in 1930.

data.text: Istanbul: "to the city"

scenes.narration: There's one danger the walls can't stop. Istanbul lies close to a major earthquake fault under the Sea of Marmara, and the city is working to strengthen its buildings.

data.text: A city on a fault line

scenes.narration: But the geography that made the city great hasn't changed in thousands of years. And it isn't going to.

data.text: The geography never changes

scenes.narration: So let's put the whole story together.

data.text: Putting the whole story together

scenes.narration: Istanbul controls the only sea route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and the shortest crossing between Europe and Asia. It has one of the best natural harbors in the region.

data.title: Why everyone wanted Istanbul
items: The only gate out of the Black Sea
The bridge between Europe and Asia

scenes.narration: That made it rich, and that made it a target. Its walls and its fleets held off attackers for a thousand years, until cannons and ships dragged over land finally broke through.

data.title: Why it was so hard to take
items: Walls that held for a thousand years

scenes.narration: That's why Istanbul was the prize every empire wanted. Not because of its gold, or its palaces, but because of where it stands: on a narrow strip of water between two seas and two continents.
